transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, I'm here because... well, it's a bit embarrassing, honestly. I've been noticing—or rather, my colleagues and my husband have been noticing—that I just can't seem to stay in my chair. Like, what brought me in is that I keep getting up in meetings or at dinner when everyone else is seated. I'll suddenly need to refill my coffee, or check a handout, or just walk to the back of the room, even though nothing is really urgent. 

Speaking of coffee, they changed the brand in the staff room last week, and it is just dreadful. It’s this dark roast that tastes almost burnt, you know? I brought my own French press in on Tuesday because I just couldn't take it anymore, but then I left it in the sink and one of the science teachers—Mr. Henderson, he's always so particular about the sink being clear—he left this passive-aggressive sticky note on it. I mean, I get it, but a sticky note? We're adults! Anyway, where was I? Oh, right, getting up. Yeah, it's just... I feel this need to move, even during dinner at home. My husband made this lovely roast on Sunday, and I think I got up three times before we even finished the carrots.
Do you find yourself feeling restless or needing to move even when you’re not in meetings or at dinner—like when you're watching TV or reading a book?

Oh, absolutely. It’s actually a bit of a problem at my book club. We meet every other Thursday—well, it used to be Tuesdays, but Susan’s daughter started taking ballet, so we had to switch to Thursdays. Susan has this gorgeous sunroom where we meet, but she has these wicker chairs that are just terribly uncomfortable, to be perfectly honest. I keep meaning to bring a cushion from home, but I always forget until I'm already pulling into her driveway. 

But anyway, yes, even there, or during quiet evenings at home with my husband, I have a really hard time just sitting quietly with a book or a movie. I try, I really do, but before I know it, I'm blurting out comments at the screen, or I'm up rustling around in the kitchen. Last week, right in the middle of a film, I decided we absolutely needed a cheese board. It was that new mystery movie set in Iceland—beautiful cinematography, really, just so stark and cold, you could practically feel the frost in the living room. But I just couldn't just sit there and watch it! So I ended up in the kitchen slicing gouda, or I'll just suddenly suggest we turn the TV off and do something else entirely, like play a board game. My husband is very patient, bless him, but I know all my bouncing around during his favorite shows drives him a little crazy.
Have you ever experienced periods where you felt unusually energetic, needed less sleep, or were more impulsive or talkative than usual?

Unusually energetic? Well, no, not really. I mean, I don't think I've ever had a time where I just didn't need to sleep. Sleep is so important, isn't it? Actually, speaking of sleep, I bought this new mattress topper a few months ago—memory foam, they said it was cooling, but honestly, I wake up sweating half the time. It's supposed to be infused with aloe or green tea or something ridiculous. My sister warned me about those foam things, she said they just trap the heat, and she was absolutely right. She lives down in Florida now, so she knows a thing or two about heat. We visited her last February, and the humidity was just unbearable, even in the winter! We went to this little seafood place on the water, and the pelicans were just right there on the dock, begging for scraps. It was charming, but... oh, what were you asking? Needing less sleep? No, I definitely need my sleep, even if that mattress topper makes it difficult. I haven't noticed anything like... like super energy or anything out of the ordinary like that. Just the usual bouncing around I always do.
Do you find it difficult to focus or stay attentive during conversations, reading, or tasks like paying bills or following a recipe?

Focus? Oh, well... no, not really. I mean, I don't think I have a problem paying attention to things, not like some of my students do. You should see them during seventh period. It's like trying to herd cats! I teach biology, and getting them to focus on cellular mitosis at 2:00 PM on a Friday is just a lost cause. I tried bringing in this really fascinating video about amoebas last week, but half of them were just staring out the window. 

Speaking of windows, the ones in my classroom are so drafty. The maintenance guy, Carl, he's a sweetheart, he really is, but he put this weather stripping up in November and it's already peeling off. It's that cheap foam stuff. I told the principal we needed proper glazing, especially since they're forecasting a really harsh winter. The farmer's almanac said we're supposed to get above-average snowfall this year. My husband bought a new snowblower in October just to be safe. It's this bright red contraption, takes up half the garage. I keep tripping over the cord when I try to get to the recycling bin. 

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, focusing. No, I don't really have trouble focusing on reading or recipes or anything like that. I can pay attention just fine, I just... I just don't like sitting still while I'm doing it.
Do you ever feel anxious, worried, or have trouble relaxing, even when there's no specific reason for it?

Anxious? Oh, no, I wouldn't say that. I don't really sit around worrying about things for no reason. I mean, there's always something to do, isn't there? Actually, speaking of having things to do, I finally got around to organizing my spice rack this weekend. It was an absolute disaster area. I had three half-empty jars of cumin, and don't even get me started on the paprika. I don't know why they make those little glass jars so hard to stack. 

I found this wonderful little wooden tiered shelf at a garage sale on Saturday. The woman selling it—I think her name was Martha, or maybe Margaret? She had the most beautiful garden. Her hydrangeas were just massive, these gorgeous deep blue blooms. She said her secret was coffee grounds and eggshells, which I've heard before, but I always forget to save my coffee grounds. My husband drinks that instant stuff anyway, which I just can't stand. It tastes like dirt, doesn't it? I have to have my French press in the morning. 

But anyway, what were you asking? Oh, feeling worried or anxious? No, not really. I don't really have trouble relaxing, I just... well, I relax by keeping busy, I suppose. But I don't feel nervous or anything like that.
Have you ever had a period lasting several days or more where you felt down, sad, or hopeless most of the time?

Down or sad? No, not really. I mean, everyone has a bad day here and there, but a whole stretch of feeling hopeless? No, I don't think so. I'm usually pretty upbeat. Actually, my neighbor, Susan, she's been feeling a bit down lately. Her daughter just moved away to college—Oregon State, I think. Or maybe University of Oregon? The one with the duck mascot. Anyway, Susan's been dealing with the empty nest thing, so I brought her over a casserole on Tuesday. Tuna noodle, with the little crispy fried onions on top. It's a classic, you know? 

I had to go to three different grocery stores just to find the right kind of egg noodles. The one on Fifth Street is completely remodeling their pasta aisle, and everything is just in boxes in the middle of the floor. It's a fire hazard, if you ask me. I almost ran my cart right into a display of canned tomatoes. They were having a sale, ten for ten dollars, but who needs ten cans of diced tomatoes at once? Unless you're making a massive batch of chili, I suppose. We used to do a chili cook-off at the school every November, but they stopped it after the incident with the fire alarm in 2018. Mr. Henderson from the history department completely burned his cornbread. 

But... oh, what was the question? Feeling sad for days at a time? No, I don't get like that. I'm too busy moving around to sit and feel hopeless.
Have you ever been told by a doctor or medical professional that you have a neurological or movement disorder, or has anything like this ever been suggested to you?

Neurological? Oh, like... Parkinson's or something? No, no doctor has ever said anything like that to me. I mean, my aunt Edna had a tremor in her hands when she got older, but she lived to be ninety-two. She was a tough old bird, Edna. She used to knit these incredible afghans, even when her hands were shaking. I still have one she made for my wedding. It's this hideous mustard yellow and brown chevron pattern—very 1980s, you know? It's been sitting in the cedar chest at the foot of our bed for thirty years. 

Actually, I need to get some more cedar blocks for that chest. Moths got into one of my good wool sweaters last winter. It was a beautiful cashmere cardigan I bought on a trip to Scotland. We went to Edinburgh for our twentieth anniversary. The castle there is just magnificent, though the walk up that hill is a real workout. My husband complained the whole way up, but the view from the top was worth it. We stopped at this little pub afterward and had the most amazing fish and chips. 

But, um, what were we talking about? Oh, doctors! No, no movement disorders or anything neurological. I'm perfectly healthy in that department. I just have a lot of energy, that's all.
